displayQuote: A pessimist is one who sees a disaster in every opportunity. An optimist sees opportunity in every disaster

meta.title: Who really said "A pessimist is one who sees a disaster in every opportunity. An optimist sees opportunity in every disaster"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: He really said it: the Detroit Free Press caught it on a golf course, 2 March 1925. But the pessimist/optimist quip was already circulating by 1919.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A pessimist is one who sees a disaster in every opportunity. An optimist sees opportunity in every disaster'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, Rockefeller said it: reported verbatim in the Detroit Free Press, 2 March 1925, when he was 85. He didn't coin the joke — that traces to 1919.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1839–1937 · Standard Oil founder and philanthropist; he was 85 when he said it
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The Detroit Free Press of 2 March 1925, in a story headlined “John D. at 85 Plays Splendid Golf Game,” reports Rockefeller giving exactly this definition mid‑round, after a poor start on a difficult hole. What is not his is the invention: the pessimist/optimist antithesis was already circulating in newspapers years before, and Rockefeller’s contribution was swapping the usual word “difficulty” for the heavier “disaster.”
answer.confidenceText: Printed in a newspaper while he was alive — though he did not coin the joke

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “John D. at 85 Plays Splendid Golf Game”
2 March 1925 — starts p. 1, quote on p. 3, col. 6
An offhand remark during a round of golf

source.excerpt: In one round, after a poor start on a difficult hole, he gave a definition of an optimist and a pessimist. “A pessimist,” he said, “is one who sees a disaster in every opportunity. An optimist sees opportunity in every disaster.” Thereupon, Mr. Rockefeller took out his midiron and made such a recovery that he was able to get on a 45 yard dog hole.
trail: The exact sentence is not a quote-book invention — it was printed while Rockefeller was alive and named him. The Detroit Free Press of 2 March 1925, under the headline “John D. at 85 Plays Splendid Golf Game,” reports him giving the definition mid-round; Quote Investigator transcribes the passage and cites it to start page 1, quote page 3, column 6 the chronology ↗.

It is not in his own book. His memoir Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (Doubleday, Page & Company, 1909) contains no pessimist/optimist antithesis at all — a full-text search turns up nothing. The closest thing in it is a flat declaration: “I am naturally an optimist” searchable full text ↗.

Nor did he originate the thought. The same chronology puts the earliest clean statement of the antithesis in 1919, from Bertram Carr, Mayor of Carlisle, with fragments running back to 1895, and Quote Investigator tentatively ascribes the saying to Carr rather than to any of the famous names later attached to it same page ↗.

Worth noting what the reference works carry: Wikiquote’s John D. Rockefeller page has no pessimist/optimist line in any section — not under sourced, not under disputed, not under misattributed. On this one the newspaper record is ahead of the quotation books, not behind them Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed as it stands in Quote Investigator’s citation of the Free Press page. The final clause reads that way in the transcription; it looks like a garbled rendering of a dog-leg hole, and we have left it rather than silently correcting a period source.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.heading: John D. Rockefeller
author.metaLine: 1839–1937 · American oil magnate, founder of Standard Oil, philanthropist
author.bio: Rockefeller founded the Standard Oil Company and ran it until 1897, keeping the nominal title of president until 1911 and remaining its largest shareholder long after he had stopped managing it. He was in full retirement by his early sixties and spent his last decades on philanthropy and on golf — the pastime that produced this remark, and that he was famously playing in 1907 when a telegram arrived announcing a record fine against Standard Oil. He was 85 and living the golf-course half of that life when a Detroit Free Press reporter took down his definition of an optimist.

copyAttribution: "A pessimist is one who sees a disaster in every opportunity. An optimist sees opportunity in every disaster." — John D. Rockefeller, reported in "John D. at 85 Plays Splendid Golf Game," The Detroit Free Press, 2 March 1925, p. 3. He said it mid-round, aged 85. He did not coin the joke: the earliest clean version of the pessimist/optimist antithesis is a 1919 remark by Bertram Carr, Mayor of Carlisle. Verified via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: The tangle around it
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is unusually clean — but this sentence sits inside a family of near-identical sayings that is one of the messiest on the internet, and the confusion runs in both directions.

items.why: “The pessimist sees the difficulty in every opportunity; the optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty” is credited to Churchill everywhere, and there is no substantive evidence he said it. Richard M. Langworth, editor of Churchill By Himself, placed it in an appendix titled “Red Herrings: False Attributions”; the Churchill credit does not appear in Quote Investigator’s record until a 1979 quotation book the chronology ↗.

items.scope: The coinage, as opposed to the sentence
items.why: Rockefeller said this wording in 1925, but he did not invent the antithesis. Quote Investigator’s earliest strong match is an 1919 remark by Bertram Carr, Mayor of Carlisle, and QI tentatively ascribes the saying to him — with fragments running back to 1895 same chronology ↗.

Edwin Mims’s 1929 book Adventurous America: A Study of Contemporary Life and Thought credited the educator and minister L. P. Jacks with a similar formulation — one more stop on a line that kept being re-assigned to whoever had said it most recently the chronology ↗.

items.scope: A different Rockefeller line, often merged with this one
items.why: “I always tried to turn every disaster into an opportunity” circulates alongside this quote and is frequently quoted as though it were the same remark. It is a separate sentence, and it is not in his 1909 memoir Random Reminiscences of Men and Events, whose full text contains no such phrasing searchable full text ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Rockefeller really did say this exact sentence — on a golf course, aged 85, in a story printed on 2 March 1925. What he supplied was the word “disaster.” The joke itself was already public property, and its earliest clean documented form belongs to a mayor of Carlisle in 1919 Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The setting matters. This is not a boardroom aphorism or a line from a memoir — it is a golf story. The Detroit Free Press reporter watching Rockefeller in March 1925 recorded that he made a poor start on a difficult hole, offered his definition of a pessimist and an optimist, and then took out his midiron and played the recovery. The quip came with a demonstration attached, which is exactly the kind of detail that makes a reported remark believable and helps it travel.

The idea, though, was already public property. By 1925 the pessimist/optimist antithesis had been knocking around print for three decades in a dozen shapes — calamity, obstacle, difficulty. Rockefeller’s edit was one word: he made it disaster. Coming from the man who had taken the news of a record antitrust fine in 1907 without leaving the golf course, that is the version that stuck to his name.
context.detailsSummary: The chain the line came out of
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology runs like this: a fragment in The Illustrated American in 1895 (“one man’s calamity is another’s opportunity”); partial versions in 1903; the earliest clean statement of the full antithesis in 1919, from Bertram Carr, Mayor of Carlisle; then a Rev. F. W. Cole version in 1921, newspaper “obstacle” variants in 1922, an “opportunity in every difficulty” version in 1923 — and then Rockefeller’s “disaster” version in 1925, with L. P. Jacks credited with a similar formulation in 1929 the chronology ↗.

The tell that nobody owned it: in 1942 H. L. Mencken put a “calamity” version into A New Dictionary of Quotations on Historical Principles and marked the author as unidentified. The Churchill credit that dominates the internet today does not surface in QI’s record until a 1979 quotation book same chronology ↗.

There is a real Rockefeller sentence in the same key, and it is in his own book. Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909) contains no pessimist/optimist epigram anywhere, but it does contain him saying plainly: “I am naturally an optimist” full text ↗.
context.pull: He gave the definition after a poor start on a difficult hole — then took out his midiron and made the recovery.
